quarterly_data.signal: HOW THE NBM CONTRACTS ARE ACTUALLY BUILT (CFO Luis Visoso): 'it's only nine months since we signed the first deal, we have eight very strong partnerships', kept deliberately few because 'we've been very selective... We want to go and be very strategic for a few of those customers.' Customer requirements run 'all the way to five years', and roughly two-thirds of the negotiating time went into the supply-demand foundation alone, because each agreement is specified 'by year, by quarter, by month' and by product mix - 'Think about TLC, QLC, high-cap, low-cap.' Only after that was pricing set: a fixed-price period with a mechanism that lets Sandisk 'capture upside if prices go up' and gives customers some downside, with the floor 'set that price in a way that was still highly attractive for us.' Enforcement is external: 'we came up with these financial guarantees with third-party financial institutions, which basically will flow those funds to us if they don't execute their part of the agreement.' CEO David Goeckeler added that in the last eight or nine months Sandisk has 'been able to shift now the predominance of our supply over the next couple of years to that more predictable model.'
quarterly_data.figure: nine months since we signed the first deal; agreements all the way to five years, detailed by year, by quarter, by month

quarterly_data.signal: THE FY2028-FY2030 TARGET MODEL WAS BUILT FROM THE CONTRACTS, NOT FROM THE MARKET (CFO): 'we didn't start with the market. We started with our relationship with our customers' - Sandisk modelled the NBM book across a range of price, renewal and expansion scenarios, modelled the non-NBM book separately 'under what reality would that part of the business we'd be operating', blended the two and picked the most likely outcome. The resulting long-term model is '80% gross margin all the way down to 50% free cash flow margin on an ongoing basis'. The CEO framed the commitment as contract-backed: 'we have enough confidence in the contracts we've signed and the way we've navigated this business that we can commit to this financial model.'
quarterly_data.figure: 80% gross margin all the way down to 50% free cash flow margin on an ongoing basis

quarterly_data.signal: HBF SILICON STATUS - DIE TAPE-OUT NOW, CUSTOMER SAMPLES NEXT YEAR (CEO): 'We're just taping out the die, and we want to get in a position where we could put samples in customers' hands next year, and then they'll figure out how to integrate it into their system, and then we'll see what the real potential is.' Positioning against HBM was made explicit: HBF is 'not necessarily a substitute, it's just different' and 'not a replacement for anything else' - it takes NAND's density scaling and twists the fundamental NAND design to raise bandwidth and endurance so inference providers can attack the memory wall, because 'AI is essentially a memory-bound problem'.

SCALE AND CAPITAL EFFICIENCY AS THE MOAT (CEO): 'Between us and our JV partner, we produce roughly a third of the world's NAND', which sets the R&D budget - 'you can roughly afford to invest R&D commensurate with your market share'. The R&D goal is explicitly capital productivity: 'How do I produce the incremental terabyte or incremental petabyte of supply with the least amount of capital?' Management also quantified how much supply growth is available without new fabs: 'just through the application of what I'll call intellectual capital, new nodal transitions, we can grow at a compounded 27% growth rate if we look at a 10-year period... that's not new CapEx.' On competition, China is characterised as 'kind of a China for China story at this point, and I expect that to continue.'
quarterly_data.figure: roughly a third of the world's NAND; compounded 27% growth rate over a 10-year period, not new CapEx
